prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) --  An Indonesian court has sentenced the alleged military commander of an al Qaeda-linked terror network to 15 years in prison. Abu Dujana is suspected of plotting attacks on the Australian Embassy and J.W. Marriott hotel in Jakarta. Abu Dujana is the alleged leader of the military wing of Jemaah Islamiyah, a group that is thought to be linked to al Qaeda. It aims to create a Muslim "superstate" across much of Southeast Asia. Dujana, a slight, wiry man, is accused of direct involvement in the Bali nightclub bombings of 2002 that killed more than 200, mostly Western, tourists. He is also suspected of plotting subsequent attacks on the Australian Embassy and J.W. Marriott hotel, both in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. Furthermore, authorities say Dujana is behind the violence in Poso, on Indonesia's eastern Sulawesi island. Fighting between Muslims and Christians periodically breaks out in the region and sometimes turns deadly. Police have accused Jemaah Islamiyah of sending armed militants to Poso. The court found Dujana guilty Monday of illegally possessing firearms and explosives, and of harboring suspected terrorists. His lawyers said they may appeal the sentence. After his arrest last June following a four-year hunt, Dujana admitted to CNN that he was Jemaah Islamiyah's military chief. But he said that happened only after the attacks on Western targets. He described Jemaah Islamiyah to CNN as "an underground organization," saying "it will continue to exist and continue to move on with its plans" to create an Islamic state under Sharia law despite his capture. "When a part of it is cut off ...there will be a replacement, it's only natural," he said. Dujana denied being involved in the Marriott Hotel attack. He told CNN that he helped fugitive suspect Noordin Top plan the attack, meeting him both before and after the devastating blast that killed 12 people and injured 150. "It's true, I did have a meeting with Noordin before the Marriott bombing but that doesn't mean I was involved in the attack," he said. "In that meeting, we're just aligning our views with each other -- there was absolutely no discussion about planning any bombing." In his CNN interview, Dujana was quick with messages of hate, calling all Westerners legitimate targets because of the actions of leaders like U.S. President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who he says are not giving Muslims the chance to be in power. Dujana studied in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan from 1988 to 1991. He told CNN that he met al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan during the fight against Soviet occupation. At the time, bin Laden was a field commander and he was an ordinary soldier, he said. Dujana said bin Laden was well respected then and helped him and others realize that it was permissible to kill people to defend Islam. "I didn't read it in the Quran," he said. " It's based on the teachings of our teachers, clerics, especially what Osama bin Laden first said." "Because of America's arrogance, many in the Muslim world know, believe, it's permissible to kill American soldiers. It's halal; it's permitted," he said. The court declared Jemaah Islamiyah a terrorist organization Monday and ordered it to pay 10 million rupiah ($1,088). Around the same time Dujana was captured last June, authorities also apprehended Jemaah Islamiyah's leader, known simply as Zarkasih. A verdict on his case is expected soon. Last week, two other top Jemaah Islamiyah leaders -- Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim -- were brought to Indonesia following their arrest in Malaysia. Both are being investigated for their possible role in fomenting violence in Poso. Terrorism expert Sidney Jones says Abdur Rohim is believed to have replaced Zarkasih as Jemaah Islamiyah leader. "It is another major blow to Jemaah Islamiyah, but difficult to tell what the impact will be," Jones told CNN via e-mail last week. "It could embolden a more militant faction. [It] could also lead to some serious reassessment within the organization about its future." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Kathy Quiano contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) —** An Indonesian court has sentenced Abu Dujana, the alleged military commander of an al Qaeda-linked terrorist network, to 15 years in prison.

Dujana is suspected of plotting attacks on the Australian Embassy and the J.W. Marriott Hotel in Jakarta. He is the alleged leader of the military wing of Jemaah Islamiyah, a group believed to have links to al Qaeda and which aims to establish a Muslim “superstate” across much of Southeast Asia.

A slight, wiry man, Dujana is accused of direct involvement in the 2002 Bali nightclub bombings, which killed more than 200 people, most of them Western tourists. He is also suspected of plotting subsequent attacks on the Australian Embassy and the J.W. Marriott Hotel, both in the Indonesian capital.

Authorities further allege that Dujana was behind violence in Poso, on Indonesia’s eastern island of Sulawesi. Fighting between Muslims and Christians periodically erupts in the region and sometimes turns deadly. Police have accused Jemaah Islamiyah of sending armed militants to Poso.

On Monday, the court found Dujana guilty of illegally possessing firearms and explosives and of harboring suspected terrorists. His lawyers said they may appeal the sentence.

Following his arrest last June after a four-year manhunt, Dujana acknowledged to CNN that he had served as Jemaah Islamiyah’s military chief. However, he said he assumed the role only after the attacks on Western targets.

He described Jemaah Islamiyah to CNN as “an underground organization,” adding that “it will continue to exist and continue to move on with its plans” to establish an Islamic state governed by Sharia law despite his capture.

“When a part of it is cut off ... there will be a replacement; it’s only natural,” he said.

Dujana denied involvement in the Marriott Hotel attack. He told CNN that he had helped fugitive suspect Noordin Top plan the attack, meeting him both before and after the devastating blast, which killed 12 people and injured 150.

“It’s true, I did have a meeting with Noordin before the Marriott bombing, but that doesn’t mean I was involved in the attack,” he said. “In that meeting, we’re just aligning our views with each other — there was absolutely no discussion about planning any bombing.”

During his CNN interview, Dujana readily expressed messages of hate, calling all Westerners legitimate targets because of the actions of leaders such as U.S. President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair, whom he accused of denying Muslims the opportunity to hold power.

Dujana studied in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan from 1988 to 1991. He told CNN that he met al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan during the fight against the Soviet occupation. At the time, Dujana said, bin Laden was a field commander, while he was an ordinary soldier.

Dujana said bin Laden was highly respected at the time and helped him and others come to believe that killing people in defense of Islam was permissible.

“I didn’t read it in the Quran,” he said. “It’s based on the teachings of our teachers, clerics, especially what Osama bin Laden first said.”

“Because of America’s arrogance, many in the Muslim world know, believe, it’s permissible to kill American soldiers. It’s halal; it’s permitted,” he said.

On Monday, the court also declared Jemaah Islamiyah a terrorist organization and ordered it to pay 10 million rupiah ($1,088).

Around the time of Dujana’s capture last June, authorities also apprehended Jemaah Islamiyah’s leader, known simply as Zarkasih. A verdict in his case is expected soon.

Last week, two other senior Jemaah Islamiyah leaders — Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim — were brought to Indonesia following their arrests in Malaysia. Both are being investigated for their possible roles in fomenting violence in Poso.

Terrorism expert Sidney Jones said Abdur Rohim is believed to have replaced Zarkasih as Jemaah Islamiyah’s leader.

“It is another major blow to Jemaah Islamiyah, but difficult to tell what the impact will be,” Jones told CNN via email last week. “It could embolden a more militant faction. [It] could also lead to some serious reassessment within the organization about its future.”

CNN’s Kathy Quiano contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) —** An Indonesian court has handed a 15-year prison term to Abu Dujana, the suspected military chief of an extremist organization associated with al Qaeda.

Dujana is believed to have led the armed branch of Jemaah Islamiyah, which seeks to establish an Islamic “superstate” governed by Sharia law across a large part of Southeast Asia. Authorities suspect him of helping plan attacks against Jakarta’s Australian Embassy and J.W. Marriott Hotel.

The thin, wiry militant has also been accused of direct participation in the 2002 bombings of Bali nightclubs, which claimed more than 200 lives, most of them Western tourists. Investigators further allege that he was connected to later attacks targeting the Australian Embassy and the Marriott, both located in the Indonesian capital.

Officials additionally say Dujana was responsible for violence in Poso, on the eastern Indonesian island of Sulawesi. The area has experienced recurring clashes between Christians and Muslims, some of which have resulted in deaths. Police allege that Jemaah Islamiyah dispatched armed fighters to the region.

On Monday, the court convicted Dujana of unlawful possession of weapons and explosives and of sheltering suspected terrorists. His attorneys indicated that they might challenge the ruling on appeal.

Dujana was arrested in June after authorities pursued him for four years. Following his capture, he acknowledged in an interview with CNN that he had served as Jemaah Islamiyah’s military commander. However, he maintained that he assumed that position only after attacks against Western targets had already occurred.

He characterized Jemaah Islamiyah as a clandestine group and said his detention would not stop it from continuing its work toward creating a Sharia-based Islamic state. According to Dujana, if one part of the organization is removed, another will naturally take its place.

Although he rejected claims that he participated in the Marriott bombing, Dujana said he had assisted fugitive suspect Noordin Top in planning the attack and had met with him both before and after the explosion, which killed 12 people and wounded 150. He insisted that their pre-bombing meeting merely involved coordinating their perspectives and included no discussion whatsoever about organizing an attack.

During the CNN interview, Dujana also voiced openly hostile views toward the West. He said all Westerners could legitimately be targeted because leaders such as then-U.S. President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair were, in his view, preventing Muslims from gaining political power.

Dujana received an education in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan between 1988 and 1991. He told CNN that, during the struggle against Soviet occupation, he met al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden. At that stage, Dujana said, bin Laden was a battlefield commander while he himself was an ordinary fighter.

According to Dujana, bin Laden was highly regarded and helped persuade him and others that killing people in defense of Islam was acceptable. Dujana said this belief did not come from his own reading of the Quran but from the instruction of religious teachers and clerics, particularly bin Laden’s statements. He further asserted that what he described as American arrogance had led many Muslims to regard the killing of U.S. soldiers as halal, or religiously permitted.

Also on Monday, the court formally designated Jemaah Islamiyah as a terrorist organization and fined it 10 million rupiah, equivalent to $1,088.

At roughly the same time as Dujana’s arrest the previous June, officials detained Jemaah Islamiyah’s leader, who is known simply as Zarkasih. A decision in his trial was expected shortly.

The week before Dujana’s sentencing, two additional senior Jemaah Islamiyah figures, Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim, were returned to Indonesia after being arrested in Malaysia. Investigators were examining whether either man had helped provoke the unrest in Poso.

Terrorism analyst Sidney Jones said Abdur Rohim was thought to have succeeded Zarkasih as the head of Jemaah Islamiyah. In an email to CNN, Jones described the development as another significant setback for the organization but said its ultimate consequences remained uncertain. She suggested that it might strengthen a more radical faction or prompt the group to seriously reconsider its direction and future.

CNN’s Kathy Quiano contributed to the report.
